unit.title: Production judgment and staff practice
unit.summary: Make iOS delivery inclusive, measurable, diagnosable, private, and reversible where the platform permits it. Build evidence of technical judgment and team impact through concrete artifacts; course completion does not confer or guarantee a staff title.

lessons.title: Make a screen readable, speakable, and usable in other languages
lessons.summary: Help people complete the task with VoiceOver, larger text, and other languages. Give dates a clear meaning and let layouts grow with their content.
objectives: Tell apart an element's spoken name, changing value, role, action, and test lookup key.
Explain how a font can grow while a fixed paragraph height still clips it.
Choose the right translation bundle and date-formatting context.
Write accessibility and language checks, and show which ones you actually performed.

sections.title: Start with the task a person needs to finish
sections.html:
Accessibility means people can use the feature through different ways of reading and interacting. VoiceOver is iOS's screen reader; it reads an accessibility representation rather than pixels. Dynamic Type is the user's text-size choice. An Android Compose semantics tree gives a useful analogy for that representation. A booking card can look right yet hide the date or an action from a person. Define success as finding, choosing, and confirming a slot, not just matching an English screenshot.

Start a synthetic appointment card with three contracts: the date has an unambiguous meaning, the primary action is discoverable and operable, and the card grows when text grows. Then add states: loading, unavailable, selected, and validation failure. Ask what is announced when each changes. This mirrors Android accessibility work, but VoiceOver gestures, UIKit properties, and SwiftUI modifiers are their own platform contracts.

A staff-level contribution can be a reusable acceptance matrix that prevents the same exclusion across several teams. It does not require rewriting every view. Choose one workflow, identify its shared components, and record which observations apply to those components versus the particular screen. Do not claim an entire application is accessible because one card works.

sections.title: Give people a name and tests a lookup key
sections.html:
An accessibility label names a control for a person. accessibilityValue describes its changing state; a hint explains an outcome that may be unclear. Traits tell VoiceOver the role, such as button, or a state, such as selected. An accessibility identifier is a stable key used by tests to find the control. It cannot replace a translated spoken name. The checkout uses identifier factories; follow that convention in real work while keeping spoken meaning separate from test lookup.

import SwiftUI

struct SyntheticSlotButton: View {
    let selected: Bool
    let choose: () -> Void

    var body: some View {
        Button(action: choose) {
            Text("Morning appointment")
        }
        .accessibilityValue(
            selected ? Text("Selected") : Text("Not selected")
        )
        .accessibilityIdentifier("synthetic.slot.morning")
    }
}

This requires a SwiftUI target; it is not a command-line Swift program. () -> Void is a closure taking no arguments and returning no meaningful value. Button(action:) forwards that closure; its label supplies a localized text key. The synthetic identifier is intentionally not a production factory. Avoid appending the word “button” to a label because the control already exposes its role.

Grouping children can help a card read coherently, but combining or ignoring children may remove separately operable actions. The checkout calendar deliberately hides its top-bar children and exposes an adjustable action. Trace both increment and decrement, including boundaries, before copying that approach. A group must retain the functionality its children previously provided.

sections.title: Let the text and its space grow together
sections.html:
Dynamic Type changes text using styles and content-size categories, or named size choices. It is more than one multiplier for every font. UIKit text styles and SwiftUI semantic fonts provide scaling rules; Android sp gives a starting analogy. A title and a caption can scale differently. At the larger accessibility categories, the layout may also need to change. A horizontal pair might become a vertical stack so both the text and the action remain readable and reachable.

import UIKit

@MainActor
func makeSyntheticTitle() -> UILabel {
    let label = UILabel()
    label.font = .preferredFont(forTextStyle: .headline)
    label.adjustsFontForContentSizeCategory = true
    label.numberOfLines = 0
    label.text = String(localized: "Appointment details")
    return label
}

This UIKit example uses String(localized:), available on iOS 15 and later. @MainActor expresses UI isolation. The external argument label forTextStyle: explains the font choice; .headline is inferred from the expected enum type. Zero lines means no line-count limit, not zero visible lines. The surrounding constraints must still permit height to increase.

Attributed text carries formatting on parts of a string, including paragraph geometry. A glyph is the drawn shape of a character. In the checkout, the font can grow while a stored maximum line height stays fixed, cutting off taller glyphs. BookingSectionView.setTitle uses the existing helper to remove that cap when sizes grow. Custom fonts still need UIFontMetrics and updates; do not rescale an already scaled font. Also let constraints and line limits permit wrapping. This one fix is not a reason to remove paragraph rules everywhere.

sections.title: Translate whole meanings in the correct bundle
sections.html:
Localization means adapting a feature to a language and its conventions. Android string and plural resources give a useful comparison. iOS uses resources such as .strings and .stringsdict in this checkout. A resource bundle is the packaged place those translations belong. Xcode 15 introduced string catalogs, a newer way to author translations and variations. Choosing catalogs changes tools and ownership. It does not remove the need to understand the existing bundle or justify a repository-wide migration.

Do not assemble a sentence from translated fragments. Word order and grammar vary. A count of available appointments needs language-specific plural categories, not an English count == 1 branch. A translator needs a comment explaining whether “Available” describes a slot, clinician, or action. Interpolation can preserve a whole translatable sentence, but the resource still needs correct variation rules and translator review.

Resource lookup is equally important. String(localized:) defaults to the main bundle. A Swift package's resources may live in its generated Bundle.module; a Tuist framework may use a different generated accessor or established bundle helper. Bundle.module is not a universal property available in every target. Inspect the module manifest and existing localization helper before choosing a bundle. A correct key in the wrong bundle often falls back to the development language, which can make English-only testing misleading.

Distinguish an ordinary runtime String from SwiftUI's localized string key or localized resource APIs. Passing a dynamically constructed string can select an overload with different localization behavior. Declare the intended type and verify the rendered result in another locale rather than assuming every Text initializer performs identical lookup.

sections.title: Keep language, time zone, and calendar separate
sections.html:
A locale chooses conventions such as language, number separators, and date presentation. A time zone maps an instant to local clock time. A calendar defines date components and day arithmetic. One does not substitute for another. An appointment can belong to a zone different from the phone's zone; showing the phone's local date might move it to a different day. State the product's appointment-zone rule before formatting. Keep that choice separate from the language used to describe the date.

Use Foundation date and number formatting rather than a manually assembled English month/day string. In a synthetic lab, fix the locale and zone for deterministic assertions, then separately test the product's runtime selection policy. A fixed locale in a test is not a recommendation to hard-code that locale in the feature. Likewise, adding 86,400 seconds is not a general way to advance a civil day across daylight-saving changes.

For layout, prefer leading and trailing semantics over left and right. Mirror directional navigation when appropriate, but do not blindly mirror logos, media controls, or all imagery. Exercise an Arabic or Hebrew locale and a pseudolocalized long-string environment. Check where truncation occurs and whether it changes meaning. Large text plus a longer translation is a distinct case, not two independent boxes that automatically compose.

Other accessibility preferences matter: sufficient contrast, differentiation beyond color, Reduce Motion, and reachable targets. A red border alone does not explain a validation error; provide text and associate the error with the field. Keep announcements useful and avoid repeated notifications that interrupt speech whenever ordinary state updates occur.

sections.title: Check pictures and actual interaction
sections.html:
Verification means collecting evidence that the task works. Automated checks catch useful mechanical failures, while manual VoiceOver use tests reading order and actions. A snapshot can show clipped text but cannot prove that a gesture reaches Confirm. Accessibility Inspector can report labels, geometry, and audit findings, yet a clean report does not prove the task makes sense. A UI test finding an identifier proves that the control can be found by that test, not that its spoken name is helpful.

Create a compact matrix with default text, the largest supported accessibility size, a long translation, a right-to-left language, and a combined large-text/long-translation case. Include a change of size while the screen is already visible; initial construction and trait updates are different paths. For custom attributed typography, inspect both font and paragraph attributes after the change.

The local calendar is useful for a review exercise because it replaces ordinary top-bar navigation with an adjustable accessibility element. Verify the month label, unavailable direction behavior, and preservation of date selection. Do not infer those behaviors from modifier names alone. Record observed speech and focus steps, the device and OS, fixture, and gaps.

Finally, make accessibility part of acceptance before implementation. If a redesign changes control grouping, establish the expected reading order and state announcements in review. This turns a late discovery into a design decision and gives future engineers a clear reason for the code.

quiz.question: A UI test finds a button by accessibilityIdentifier, but VoiceOver announces a cryptic internal token. What should you inspect first?
options: The spoken label and the control's semantics
The simulator's network latency
Whether the identifier is globally unique across every screen
quiz.explanation: The identifier serves test lookup. VoiceOver obtains the element's user-facing semantics from its label, value, traits, and actions. A stable automation token cannot substitute for a localized label.

quiz.question: A UIKit attributed title scales its font but clips at accessibility sizes. Which diagnosis fits the checkout example?
options: Dynamic Type cannot support attributed strings
A frozen maximum paragraph line height can constrain the enlarged glyphs
numberOfLines must always be one
quiz.explanation: The active helper explicitly removes an inappropriate maximum-line-height cap at larger sizes. Font scaling and paragraph geometry are separate; constraints and line limits also need inspection.

quiz.question: A framework translation exists, but a localized string remains English. What is a plausible cause?
options: The development language is always mandatory
Right-to-left layout disables translation
Lookup uses the main bundle while the resource belongs to the framework
quiz.explanation: Localization lookup needs the correct resource bundle and table. Bundle.module is appropriate only where SwiftPM generates it; inspect the actual target's resource conventions.

exercise.brief: Design a made-up appointment card and its acceptance checks. Read the calendar top bar and booking-title helper. Keep patient data and client edits out of the exercise.
steps: Draw the title, date, slot selection, and Confirm action. Write the expected VoiceOver reading and action order.
Describe the layout at accessibility text sizes, including a size change while the screen is visible.
Choose the translation owner, plural rules, locale, calendar, appointment zone, and right-to-left layout behavior.
Read each repo anchor. Explain one reason a generic label change cannot replace its existing behavior.
Create five rows of checks. Label each as planned or actually performed, and attach observations when available.
acceptance: Every interactive action remains reachable through the proposed accessibility representation
Test identifiers and spoken strings have different responsibilities
The typography plan covers paragraph geometry and changing traits
The localization plan owns complete sentences and the correct bundle
Evidence and verification gaps are explicitly labeled
exercise.solution:
The worked card gives the heading, appointment time, selectable slot, and Confirm action their own meaningful elements. A selected slot keeps a useful name and exposes a changing selected value. It never reads its test identifier as its label. An unavailable slot explains why it cannot be chosen. After confirmation, focus should move to the outcome or error under a tested rule, without repeated announcements interrupting the person.

The card becomes vertical at accessibility sizes, removes fixed text heights, and lets labels wrap. For the existing booking title, use the established dynamic-line-height route rather than assigning a newly styled attributed string directly. A review note records that the helper addresses a paragraph cap, while the surrounding view still owns constraints.

CaseExpected evidence
Default EnglishNo clipping; all actions reached in task order
Largest accessibility textVertical flow; full title; confirm remains reachable
Long translationComplete localized sentence and correct plural variation
Right-to-leftLeading/trailing layout and sensible date navigation
Long translation plus live text-size changeNo stale paragraph cap after traits update

The date policy states “show the appointment's zone and disclose it when ambiguous.” Resource ownership follows the target that owns the card, using that target's bundle accessor. For the calendar top bar, a review verifies that adjustable actions preserve both directions and respect bounds. This worked artifact demonstrates the reasoning; it supplies no claim of a completed device audit. Your submission must add the actual observations or explicitly leave those rows unverified.

simple.story: At a station, Priya needs the next train time and the boarding gate. One sign has large print. Another sign uses her language. A speaker reads the gate name, and the gate button has a clear action. If the speaker says only the maintenance code “gate_07_btn,” she still cannot tell what to do. lessons.title: Performance: ask what is slow, then measure the cause
lessons.summary: Turn a slow-screen report into a repeatable experiment. Choose the right tool, mark the right interval, and report behavior checks and measurement limits.
objectives: Tell apart waiting time, CPU work, drawing, memory use, and energy cost.
Choose an Instruments tool for a claim you can test and disprove.
Mark a timed interval with a matching end and limited safe metadata.
Compare before and after under the same conditions, preserve behavior, and state what remains unmeasured.

sections.title: Choose where the stopwatch starts and ends
sections.html:
An interval is the time between two named events. Start with a person's complaint: “the result list takes too long to become usable.” Choose whether to measure the tap to usable results or the screen appearing to a responsive interaction. Those are different intervals. Android Perfetto can separate CPU work from waiting. Instruments provides related investigation tools on Apple platforms with different tracks and rules. A total stopwatch time alone cannot tell whether the delay came from computation, a network wait, or drawing.

Specify the device class, OS, app configuration, fixture, cache state, and network conditions. A debug simulator run is useful for finding a path, but its timings do not represent release behavior on a phone. Simulator CPU and memory characteristics come from the host. Profiling overhead also changes the workload; compare equivalent conditions and use less intrusive confirmation measurements after diagnosis.

Write one hypothesis before opening a trace: “Repeated uniqueness checks on the main actor grow quadratically with result count.” Then state a falsifier: “If Time Profiler shows little CPU in that path, or the interval is dominated by I/O waiting, this is not the primary cause.” A hypothesis protects you from optimizing whichever function name happens to look familiar.

sections.title: Pick a tool that can answer the question
sections.html:
Time Profiler samples call stacks: snapshots of which functions are executing. It helps find CPU work, the time the processor spends running code. A frequently sampled stack is a clue, not an exact count of calls. Waiting for a network response can take a long elapsed time while using little CPU. Compare the relevant interval and thread tracks with the call tree. The largest row in that tree is not automatically the reason the person waited.

For interaction stalls, inspect main-thread activity and responsiveness using the appropriate Instruments template and available hang or animation tracks. A 60 Hz display has about 16.7 milliseconds between refreshes; 120 Hz has about 8.3. Those numbers describe refresh cadence, not a universal allowance for your code: input, layout, rendering, and other system work share the pipeline. A single successful frame does not establish smooth scrolling.

Allocations helps investigate allocation rate and retained objects; Memory Graph helps explore references; Leaks identifies some leak patterns. Retained memory can be a legitimate cache or an unintended ownership cycle, and not every growth pattern is a leak. Repeatedly enter and leave the workflow, then inspect whether the population settles. Use device memory-pressure evidence when diagnosing termination, rather than importing the simulator's apparent limit.

Energy is another axis. Polling less often or coalescing work may improve battery use without changing an isolated CPU benchmark. Choose the tool and runtime environment that answer the question, and state which costs your experiment deliberately leaves unresolved.

sections.title: Mark one operation with a start and an end
sections.html:
A signpost is a marker your app places in a trace. A start and matching end make one operation visible on the timeline. The synthetic example uses OSSignposter from Apple's os module, available on iOS 15 and macOS 12 or later. It is separate from the checkout's Honeycomb tracer. The two systems may investigate related work, but have their own recording, sampling, and export rules. This example does not claim to implement the repository's telemetry API.

import os

@available(iOS 15.0, macOS 12.0, *)
func stableUniqueIDs(_ ids: [String]) -> [String] {
    let signposter = OSSignposter(
        subsystem: "example.course", category: "ResultMapping"
    )
    let state = signposter.beginInterval(
        "UniqueIDs", id: signposter.makeSignpostID()
    )
    defer { signposter.endInterval("UniqueIDs", state) }

    var seen = Set<String>()
    return ids.filter { seen.insert($0).inserted }
}

The underscore before ids removes the external label, so the call is stableUniqueIDs(values). Set<String> stores membership, and insert returns a tuple whose inserted field tells whether this is the first occurrence. $0 is the filter closure's element. Filtering the original array preserves first-occurrence order; converting a set directly to an array would not preserve that contract.

The interval state pairs this start with its end; defer runs when this synchronous function exits. An asynchronous operation needs an interval whose lifetime covers completion, cancellation, and failure rather than merely task creation. Use bounded names and synthetic or approved metadata. Never embed an appointment description, token, or user query in a signpost name.

sections.title: Fix the cause without breaking ownership
sections.html:
The main actor owns UI state, and costly synchronous work there can delay interaction. Starting Task inside main-actor code normally inherits that actor. It does not automatically move a sorting loop elsewhere. await allows a pause; it does not promise a background thread. First ask whether a better algorithm removes the cost. If you need another worker boundary, decide who owns its lifetime, how cancellation reaches it, and which Sendable values cross to it.

Often an algorithmic fix is simpler than introducing concurrency. A baseline that scans the growing output array with contains for every identifier has quadratic worst-case comparisons. A membership set usually gives expected linear membership work across the list, subject to hashing and equality costs, and uses extra memory. The example retains array ordering while separating that membership concern. Strings are variable-length values, so do not present these complexity claims as a guarantee of identical constant cost per identifier.

Other common suspects need different fixes: full-resolution image decoding, date formatter creation per cell, repeated layout invalidation, and synchronous disk reads during interaction. Cache only when invalidation is understood. A locale-sensitive formatter needs a policy for locale, calendar, and zone changes; a cache that returns stale appointment times is not a successful optimization.

Check object ownership after moving work. A long-lived closure capturing a controller may keep an entire screen alive; weakening a capture without defining cancellation can silently discard results. Improvement means preserving behavior, lifetime, and correctness while reducing the measured cost.

sections.title: Compare like runs and check the answer
sections.html:
A benchmark measures one defined workload under stated conditions. XCTest offers metrics such as elapsed time through XCTClockMetric and CPU work through XCTCPUMetric. If you are measuring only mapping, build the fixture, or test input, before the timed block. If setup matters to the person's delay, measure that larger interval separately. Check correctness too. A candidate that silently drops required results can look fast while failing the task.

Control iterations and warm-up through the performance test's options and documented execution environment. The launch-specific XCTOSSignpostMetric.applicationLaunch measures a different boundary from an ordinary code-block clock metric. Define “warm” precisely: process startup, populated disk caches, and a previously installed app are different conditions. A cached process launch and a cold installation are different experiments. Trace the selected test target, superclass, options, and runner before asserting the sample count; a source comment or a file in the tree is not proof of active execution.

A distribution shows how repeated runs differ. With a small sample, retain every value and report the count, median, range, and conditions. A p95 is the value below which about 95 percent of results lie; a handful of runs gives a very unstable estimate. Alternate baseline and candidate runs if the device may warm up. Keep build settings and input size equal, and say whether a profiler was attached. Choose a comparison your sample can actually support.

A CI baseline is valuable for detecting changes on the same runner setup, but simulator variance can create false alarms. Choose a budget with observed variance and user relevance, preserve the raw result bundle, and review unexpected changes before repeatedly relaxing a threshold.

sections.title: Write enough evidence for someone to repeat it
sections.html:
A performance report is a record of what you asked, tested, and learned. Name the problem, timed boundary, hypothesis, fixture, device, OS, build, interval, change, behavior checks, before/after samples, and cost of the change. A hypothesis is a proposed cause you can test. Local signposts explain a recording; field traces can describe how often users encounter a path. Neither automatically provides the other's coverage. State which evidence you collected and which question it can answer.

The checkout's Performance namespace holds a shared tracer, and its search extension supplies bounded contextual tags. Read those entry points to understand existing vocabulary before adding a new measurement in real feature work. Do not infer a measured benefit, sampling rate, or dashboard definition solely from the presence of a tracer.

Your recommendation should state the next uncertainty. For example: “The mapping benchmark improves, but first usable results on a low-end device remains unmeasured.” That statement is more useful than calling the feature fast. A clear boundary prevents a narrow optimization from being marketed as an end-to-end result.

Staff practice adds leverage: make the experiment template reusable, teach a teammate to reproduce it, and arrange ownership of the budget. Avoid a permanent instrumentation layer with no consumer or alerting action. Measurements earn their maintenance cost when they change decisions.

quiz.question: A result operation takes two seconds, but Time Profiler shows little CPU in its interval. What follows?
options: The CPU sampling tool is definitely broken
Elapsed time may be dominated by waiting; inspect I/O, suspension, or synchronization
Rewrite every model as a reference type
quiz.explanation: Elapsed time includes waiting. Sampled execution stacks describe CPU work and cannot alone explain every delay. Correlate the interval with tasks, requests, and thread activity.

quiz.question: Why does the set-backed filter preserve an important property that Array(Set(ids)) would lose?
options: It preserves first-occurrence order from the input
It guarantees constant memory
It eliminates string hashing
quiz.explanation: The array traversal retains original ordering while the set answers membership. An unordered set conversion does not express that ordering guarantee, and the optimization still consumes memory and performs hashing.

quiz.question: Does Task created in a @MainActor context guarantee that expensive synchronous work leaves the main actor?
options: Yes, Task always creates a private thread
Yes, if there is any await later
No; reason about inherited isolation and the actual work boundary
quiz.explanation: A task is a concurrency unit rather than a promise of a background thread. Inherited actor isolation can leave synchronous CPU work on the main actor; awaiting something later does not undo that blocking.

exercise.brief: Investigate first-occurrence deduplication with 10,000 made-up IDs. Compare the array-scan baseline with a set-backed candidate, then plan a separate screen timing experiment.
steps: Write the baseline using output.contains and the candidate using a set for membership.
Check full output order, empty input, repeated IDs, and exact case-sensitive equality.
Create the same fixture outside both timed blocks.
Name an Instruments interval and a confirmation experiment using a release build on a device.
Write a report with actual retained samples or clearly empty sample slots. Explain extra memory use and the still-open screen-delay question.
acceptance: The candidate has the same output contract as the baseline
The report fixes fixture, configuration, cache state, and environment
Measurement boundaries and correctness assertions are separate
No synthetic timing is represented as a local or production observation
The recommendation includes memory and user-visible validation
exercise.solution:
The baseline keeps an ID only when the output does not yet contain it. For ["b", "a", "b", "c"], both implementations must return ["b", "a", "c"]. Check empty, all-equal, and all-distinct inputs as well. This contract uses exact Swift string equality: "A" and "a" remain different. A faster implementation must not add case folding or lose first-occurrence order.

The report hypothesis is “Membership scans dominate the mapping interval as distinct count increases.” Compare identical fixtures at several sizes so that the growth pattern is visible. The candidate uses a set for membership and the input array for order. Its tradeoff is extra membership storage; reserve capacity only if a representative experiment justifies it.

import XCTest

// Add to an isolated XCTest target that contains stableUniqueIDs.
@available(iOS 15.0, macOS 12.0, *)
final class SyntheticMappingPerformanceTests: XCTestCase {
    func testMappingTime() {
        let input = (0..<10_000).map { "id-\($0 % 2_000)" }
        var output: [String] = []
        measure(metrics: [XCTClockMetric()]) {
            output = stableUniqueIDs(input)
        }
        XCTAssertEqual(output.count, 2_000)
        XCTAssertEqual(output.first, "id-0")
    }
}

This worked test demonstrates setup placement and post-measurement correctness checks; the full behavioral tests must compare all ordering expectations separately. The example has not been executed as an iOS target. A report can show illustrative median values of 94 ms baseline and 37 ms candidate, but must label them synthetic demonstration values, not measured results. Replace them with the retained samples from your own experiment. Next measure action-to-usable-results on a device: network delay and rendering may dwarf this isolated change. Only that second boundary supports a claim about the screen.

simple.story: Omar runs a small tea stall. A customer waits while the kettle warms, the cups are found, and the tea is poured. Omar first assumes finding cups is slow. He times that step separately from the full order. A new shelf makes finding cups quicker, but the kettle still takes most of the wait. The change helps one step; it has not yet proved that customers receive tea sooner. He repeats the same order with the same kettle and records every trial before deciding what to improve next.

lessons.title: Reliability: count outcomes and read the right diagnostic
lessons.summary: Define whether the task succeeded, then choose the evidence for a crash, hang, or failed request. Keep matching symbols and prove recovery in the affected group.
objectives: Define what counts as an attempt and compare success and failure in named groups.
Tell apart Swift errors, exceptions, hangs, watchdog stops, and memory-pressure stops.
Explain how matching binary UUIDs and dSYMs turn crash addresses into source names.
Write an incident note with safe data, evidence, containment, and checks that support recovery.

sections.title: Count completed tasks, not just crash events
sections.html:
Reliability means the person's task works correctly, including recovery when something fails. A booking feature can stay alive while every submission fails. Crash counts alone would miss that. Android crash and ANR experience helps, but an iOS process stop, a hang, and a thrown operation error are different events. Begin with the product outcome: the booking completes correctly, failures are handled, and a repeated request does not create duplicate work. Then decide which signals can show that outcome.

Define the operation and its denominator. “Successful confirmed appointments divided by eligible submission attempts” means something different from “HTTP 2xx responses divided by requests.” A server acceptance can precede confirmation, while retry traffic can inflate request counts. Define eligibility, duplicates, cancellation, timeout, and the point at which success is known before writing a dashboard query.

A cohort is a named group you compare, such as one build on one OS version. Use approved version, build, device-family, feature-group, and operation-state fields. Keep their possible values limited: fixed outcome codes are easier to compare than arbitrary error descriptions. Use the same population and time window before and after a fix. An overall rate can improve while a smaller OS group still fails badly.

Logs, traces, and metrics serve different questions. A log captures a fact, a trace connects steps in one operation, and a metric summarizes a population. Use all three deliberately rather than asking a stream of unstructured messages to provide every answer.

sections.title: Name the failure before opening a report
sections.html:
A Swift Error is a value that code can throw and catch. An Objective-C exception, a fatal trap, and an operating-system termination are different mechanisms. A trap stops execution after an invalid operation, such as an out-of-bounds access. do/catch does not turn every process failure into an ordinary Swift error. A watchdog stops an app that misses a required responsiveness or lifecycle deadline. Choose a diagnostic artifact that matches the failure instead of treating every stop as the same crash.

ObservationUseful artifact
Swift operation throwsTyped error, operation context, trace, safe logs
Fatal trap or invalid memory accessCrash report and matching symbols
Interface stops respondingHang diagnostics and main-thread timeline
Watchdog terminationTermination reason, lifecycle context, relevant stacks
Memory-pressure terminationJetsam report and memory investigation

Jetsam reports describe memory pressure and processes; they are not ordinary crash backtraces waiting for symbolication. A watchdog report concerns failure to satisfy a responsiveness or lifecycle deadline. Do not import Android ANR timing assumptions or claim one universal timeout for every iOS state.

Cancellation deserves its own category. Navigation away may intentionally cancel a load; treating that as a server outage corrupts the reliability measure. Conversely, suppressing all cancellation-looking errors can hide operations unexpectedly abandoned by an ownership bug. Define which cancellations are expected and where the reason is established.

sections.title: Use a short, fixed set of outcome names
sections.html:
A bounded classification maps many inputs to a small, known set of outcome names. That makes rates easier to compare without exporting arbitrary error text. The synthetic Swift function below classifies only a transport result. It calls no server or telemetry service. Keeping the function small makes its assumptions visible: whether the caller canceled, whether a response exists, and which status range it belongs to. Those facts alone do not decide whether a booking was confirmed.

enum TransportOutcome: String {
    case responseAccepted, clientRejected, serverFailed
    case noResponse, cancelled, unexpectedResponse
}

func classifyTransport(
    status: Int?, intentionallyCancelled: Bool
) -> TransportOutcome {
    if intentionallyCancelled { return .cancelled }
    guard let status = status else { return .noResponse }
    switch status {
    case 200..<300: return .responseAccepted
    case 400..<500: return .clientRejected
    case 500..<600: return .serverFailed
    default: return .unexpectedResponse
    }
}

Int? can be absent. guard let unwraps it and exits the function if absent, unlike a force unwrap that can trap. 200..<300 includes 200 and excludes 300. TransportOutcome: String assigns stable raw strings to the cases. The two external labels make the cancellation assumption explicit at a call site.

This is a transport classification, not a booking-success rule. A real design needs application-level outcomes, authentication distinctions, retryability, and finer reasons within unexpected response ranges. A present but unexpected response remains different from receiving no response. “Client rejected” does not prove the user did anything wrong. Nor does no response prove the server never committed a request; reconciliation or an idempotency contract may be needed after a timeout.

When exporting telemetry, map this bounded enum through the established reporter. Do not send an entire request, response, URL query, or error object by default. An allowlist of safe fields is easier to review than assuming that all vendor SDK defaults are appropriate.

sections.title: Match symbols to the exact binary
sections.html:
Symbolication replaces machine addresses in a crash report with function and source names. A dSYM is the debug-symbol file that supplies that mapping. Keep it with the archive for the binary you distributed. Its UUID, or unique binary identifier, must match the report's corresponding image. The version text alone cannot establish that match. Rebuilding the same commit may produce another UUID, so a later rebuild cannot replace the original symbols. Frameworks and extensions also need their own matches.

Read the report's app/build identity, architecture, OS, exception or termination type, triggered thread, application-specific information when present, and binary images. Then symbolicate through the supported Xcode workflow or tools. A non-top frame may be the first meaningful application frame; runtime machinery often appears above it. All threads can matter, particularly for synchronization and watchdog investigations.

A symbolicated line is evidence of execution at failure, not automatically the defect. Invalid memory access can originate earlier, and concurrency bugs can depend on ordering that the final stack does not reveal. Cluster similar signatures, assess frequency by cohort, and seek a reproduction that supports a mechanism.

Keep a distinction between evidence and hypothesis in the incident note. “The triggered thread contains synthetic mapper code” is evidence. “The mapper used an outdated index after data replacement” is a hypothesis until you trace the state transition or reproduce it. Record missing symbols as a diagnostic gap rather than inventing a source location.

sections.title: Missing reports do not prove health
sections.html:
Coverage is which failures or operations your evidence can actually observe. Organizer diagnostics, MetricKit, and third-party reporters have different paths and gaps. MetricKit delivers supported system-collected metrics and diagnostics to an app subscriber; it does not synchronously report every user action. Availability and delivery depend on payload and OS. Read the current API contract when implementing it. This checkout lesson does not claim MetricKit is installed. State collection limits before interpreting a quiet dashboard as a healthy feature.

Third-party crash capture also has limits. A process can be killed before the reporter persists or exports data. A crash-free-session percentage depends on the SDK's session definition, consent, collection, and sampling; it is not automatically the fraction of users who successfully completed the product task. Missing data is not proof of health.

The active app startup configures Sentry and the shared tracing path. Its beforeSend callback is inside #if DEBUG and suppresses certain local events. That is a build-conditional local diagnostic behavior, not evidence of production redaction. The active error adapter attaches contextual tags and captures an event; inspect data flow and access controls before expanding it.

Define what happens when telemetry is unavailable: buffer within a bounded budget, drop deliberately, and avoid turning diagnostics into another reliability problem. An error handler that blocks the UI or throws while reporting can worsen the original incident.

sections.title: Limit harm, fix the cause, then check recovery
sections.html:
Containment limits harm while the cause is still being investigated. It might pause rollout, disable a compatible feature, reduce a risky server path, or offer a safer fallback. Name the owner and affected clients for each action. A remote flag cannot protect a launch failure reached before the app reads that flag. Pausing store rollout cannot replace copies already installed. Repair changes the failing mechanism. Recovery then needs evidence that the same affected group can complete the task again.

Repair addresses the mechanism. Prefer a minimal fix with a regression test for the failing transition. For a suspected stale index, a test should replace the data before selection handling and verify identifier-based behavior, not merely exercise the happy path with the original array. For memory pressure, test repeated workflow entry and measure whether retention stabilizes.

Recovery evidence must use the same cohort and denominator as the incident. Monitor both failure rate and successful task completion; a crash decrease caused by users abandoning the feature is not recovery. Explain telemetry delay and minimum volume before declaring stability.

A useful post-incident artifact records impact window, known affected cohorts, evidence, hypotheses considered, containment scope, fix verification, owner, and follow-up. Avoid blame and overconfident certainty. The staff contribution is reducing future diagnostic and coordination cost, such as preserving symbols automatically or standardizing failure contracts across modules.

quiz.question: Why can a dSYM rebuilt from the same source commit fail to symbolicate an old crash?
options: Swift cannot provide line numbers
Symbolication requires matching binary-image UUIDs, which a rebuild may change
The app version must always be zero
quiz.explanation: Source identity and binary identity are different. Retain the distributed archive and each matching dSYM; verify UUIDs against the crash's binary images.

quiz.question: Will do/catch around a screen load catch an operating-system jetsam termination?
options: Yes, as CancellationError
Yes, if the load is async
No; jetsam is a process termination with a different diagnostic artifact
quiz.explanation: Swift error handling covers thrown Error values. Jetsam occurs under memory pressure and is investigated through jetsam reports and memory tools, not as a caught Swift error.

quiz.question: A request timed out. Is immediately retrying a non-idempotent submission always safe?
options: No; the server may have committed it despite the missing response
Yes; timeout proves no server execution
Yes; retries make the denominator irrelevant
quiz.explanation: The absence of a response does not establish absence of server-side effects. An idempotency key or reconciliation protocol is needed for operations where duplicate submission matters.

exercise.brief: Write an incident note for a made-up build with three cases: a trap, a memory-pressure termination, and a slow request that does not terminate the app. Keep their evidence paths separate.
steps: Define eligible attempts, confirmed success, expected cancellation, and build/OS groups.
Choose a diagnostic artifact for each case and list what you need before claiming a cause.
Allow only fixed safe state and failure fields in your proposed event, rather than copying request payloads.
Write containment actions and say which installed clients each can actually affect.
Choose one hypothesis. Plan a regression test for it and a recovery check after release.
acceptance: The artifact does not treat all three cases as ordinary crashes

The outcome metric has an explicit denominator
Containment has an owner and an affected-client boundary
Hypotheses, observations, and synthetic numbers remain distinguishable
exercise.solution:
This worked note counts a submission only after an authenticated person confirms it and the client accepts the attempt. Retries use the same approved logical-operation identity so they do not inflate the count. Navigation cancellation before submission is separate. A timeout afterward stays unresolved until reconciliation checks what happened. Success requires receiving and presenting the confirmed state; an HTTP success alone is not enough.

Case A has a symbolicated trap report for synthetic build 410. The matching dSYM UUID is verified; a mapper frame suggests a stale-index hypothesis. The proposed regression test replaces the result array before a delayed selection callback and verifies lookup by stable ID. That test supports the mechanism only after reproducing the failure in the candidate code. Case B has a jetsam report without an application backtrace: investigate repeated image retention and device memory pressure with allocation and ownership evidence. Case C stays alive but times out: follow its trace and reconcile server state before retrying.

The schema allows app/build, coarse OS cohort, operation state, bounded outcome code, and duration bucket. It excludes names, appointment details, tokens, and response bodies. Any operation identifier must receive its own access and retention review rather than being assumed anonymous.

Containment owner: release captain for rollout pause, feature owner for compatible flag disablement, service owner for reconciliation. Pausing does not downgrade build 410, and a remote flag cannot protect a path reached before flag retrieval. The recovery check compares confirmed-success rate and trap incidence within the same build/OS cohort after the fix, with enough attempts and an allowance for reporting delay. All incident data here is synthetic; your report must attach actual artifacts before claiming a diagnosed production defect.

simple.story: A parcel desk counts how many deliveries were confirmed. Three visitors ask about a parcel but leave before submitting it. Ten others hand over parcels. Eight get delivery confirmations; two are still unresolved. The desk should report eight confirmed out of ten submitted, while tracking the three abandoned enquiries separately. Counting only complaints could make the desk look healthy when nobody receives parcels. Counting every phone call as a new parcel would make repeated enquiries distort the result. The clerk first defines the task, then counts its outcomes.
simple.meaning: A reliability rate needs a clear denominator: the attempts included in the calculation. Requests, sessions, cancellations, and confirmed product outcomes are different populations.

example.after: The rate is 8 / 10 = 80%. The three pre-submission cancellations are tracked separately; the two unresolved submissions are not called successes or safely retried without reconciliation.

lessons.title: Security and privacy: follow secrets across each boundary
lessons.summary: Name the data you protect and how it could escape. Choose Keychain access rules, validate untrusted inputs, and make privacy declarations match real data flows.
objectives: For one feature, name the protected assets, possible attackers, trust boundaries, and checks.
Tell apart Keychain item access, Secure Enclave key operations, and Android Keystore.
Explain transport protection, identity, resource authorization, and link validation as separate defenses.
Review privacy manifests and exported data without treating one declaration as proof of compliance.

sections.title: Name what matters and how it could be harmed
sections.html:
An asset is something worth protecting. A threat model asks who could harm it, what they can do, and where a control can stop them. Your Android security habits transfer as these questions. In a made-up appointment feature, the assets include session secrets, appointment details, pending submission correctness, and operational records. They have different exposure paths and needs. Start with one concrete feature rather than a list of defenses. The model should make the failure and its check clear enough to review.

Define the attacker model. A malicious external app supplying a crafted link, an observer of logs, and a person with an unlocked device have different capabilities. A compromised service is a different boundary again. State assumptions about device compromise rather than claiming that ordinary application controls defeat every possible attacker.

Draw a simple flow: external link to navigation validation, UI to session store, client to authenticated service, response to local cache, and event to telemetry collector. Mark where input changes trust level and who authorizes access. The client can guide and validate a request, but the service must enforce authorization for the actual resource. Hiding a button is not an access-control boundary.

A useful threat row names the asset, entry point, attacker capability, failure, mitigation, and verification. “Use encryption” is incomplete; “session token written to diagnostics; restrict exported fields and assert token absence in a synthetic capture” is reviewable.

sections.title: Store a secret under a chosen access policy
sections.html:
Keychain stores items such as passwords and keys under access controls. Android Keystore often protects key material used for cryptographic operations. Apple's Secure Enclave supports particular key operations and policies. These facilities are related but are not identical. Saving a token string in Keychain does not turn that string into a Secure Enclave key. Choose the item's access policy from the feature's need, including whether it must read the secret while the device is locked or after a device migration.

Keychain item identity includes class and attributes such as service and account, with access groups controlled through entitlements. Availability attributes determine whether an item can be read while locked or after first unlock and whether it migrates to another device. WhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly fits some foreground-only secrets but prevents migration to another device. A background feature may need a different availability policy and a reason to accept that tradeoff.

Keychain calls return OSStatus; distinguish item-not-found from access or entitlement errors. If every failure is converted to “logged out,” a signing regression or locked-device condition can appear as credential loss. Updates, duplicate-item behavior, deletion scope, and concurrent access need a coherent wrapper contract.

The checkout has a query builder and an update-then-add save path. Its exposed attribute enum does not include an explicit accessibility policy. That is a review question, not proof of insecure storage: Apple documents a default when-unlocked policy, and actual requirements and call sites must be inspected. Do not change a shared wrapper's protection class globally without understanding its consumers.

sections.title: Read the Keychain query as data
sections.html:
A query describes which Keychain item to find or change. At the Security framework boundary, Swift supplies a dictionary of attribute names and values. That flexible dictionary connects to a C-based API, so its type does not prove that every combination is valid. The snippet below uses only made-up service and account names. It performs no Keychain write and contains no secret bytes. You can inspect it on macOS with Foundation and Security without creating real credential data.

import Foundation
import Security

func syntheticPasswordAttributes() -> [String: Any] {
    [
        kSecClass as String: kSecClassGenericPassword,
        kSecAttrService as String: "example.course.synthetic",
        kSecAttrAccount as String: "synthetic-session",
        kSecAttrAccessible as String:
            kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly
    ]
}

[String: Any] is a dictionary whose values can have different types. as String bridges framework constants to the dictionary key type. This dynamic dictionary is used at a C-based framework boundary; it does not give the same compile-time guarantees as a typed Swift model. A production wrapper should validate combinations, bridge to CFDictionary where needed, inspect statuses, and apply the appropriate add, update, or lookup operation.

The function intentionally contains no secret bytes. Adding kSecValueData is part of a real storage operation, but copying a dictionary does not establish a safe lifecycle. Define logout and account-switch behavior, revoke service credentials where required, and scope deletion to the application's intended items. Never copy a broad “delete all generic passwords” test helper into production.

Do not rely on uninstall as a guaranteed credential-cleanup protocol. Define application behavior when an item survives installation changes, when restoration omits a device-only item, and when a locked device temporarily prevents access. Test these scenarios with synthetic accounts and explicit state expectations.

sections.title: A protected connection is one layer of trust
sections.html:
App Transport Security, or ATS, applies platform network protection policies to supported paths. TLS protects the connection and checks the server under trust-evaluation rules. Authentication establishes identity; authorization decides whether that identity may access this resource. Those are different promises. A valid protected connection cannot prove that the caller owns a particular appointment. The service must check that access. If an endpoint fails ATS, investigate the cause rather than adding a broad exception that weakens unrelated connections.

Certificate or public-key pinning can address some attacker models but adds operational obligations: certificate rotation, backup pins or recovery, expiry, and handling clients that remain installed for months. A broken pin can disable a feature before remote configuration is reachable. Choose it from the threat model and maintenance capability, not as a reflexive checkbox. Never replace trust evaluation with an unconditional accept callback.

OAuth-style flows need their actual protocol protections, redirect validation, and state checks. An embedded client cannot keep a packaged shared secret confidential against someone inspecting the binary. A value injected at build time may hide from source control but still be recoverable from the distributed app. Classify public client identifiers separately from server credentials.

Treat incoming links, pasteboard data, and web content as untrusted. Parse a route into a bounded model, validate supported identifiers and state, and authorize any operation at the service. Universal links associate domains and apps but do not make every parameter trustworthy. Never turn a link directly into an authenticated destructive action merely because its host looks familiar.

sections.title: Collect less before data leaves the feature
sections.html:
Privacy includes deciding which data is needed, where it is kept, who receives it, and when it is deleted. Encryption addresses only part of that promise. Diagnostics can accidentally create another copy of sensitive details through URLs, error text, screenshots, or request bodies. Follow each field from collection through storage and export. Ask whether a fixed outcome code would answer the operational question without sending the appointment details. The safest review starts before unnecessary data reaches a reporter.

An allowlist exports only fields you deliberately approve. Prefer fixed outcome and build fields to arbitrary descriptions. A hashed identifier can still connect a person's activity across events, and simple values can sometimes be guessed from hashes. Hashing does not automatically make data anonymous. SDK filtering and log redaction also cover different paths. The checkout's DEBUG-only event hook is a local build behavior; inspect the production export path before claiming a privacy guarantee.

For local data, consider file protection, backup policy, shared containers, and account-switch cleanup. UserDefaults is appropriate for ordinary preferences, not a general secret store. File encryption or Keychain storage does not excuse overcollection or unrestricted telemetry export. Review the privacy boundary of dependencies, including SDK defaults and newly enabled features.

Use synthetic patient-like fixtures in development and this course. Do not paste real health or account data into an RFC, benchmark, screenshot, or incident note. This is engineering instruction rather than a legal assessment; company policy and a qualified privacy review remain the authority for regulated-data decisions.

sections.title: Make declarations describe actual behavior
sections.html:
A privacy manifest is a bundled property-list file named PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy. It declares applicable data practices and reasons for certain API uses. It is separate from permission explanations in Info.plist, App Store privacy information, and the system's runtime permission prompt. A declared reason is not permission to collect arbitrary data. Review the manifest against the app and its dependencies, then inspect the distributed artifact. Source inclusion shows packaging intent; it does not prove that every final declaration is complete or correct.

The checkout's manifest contains entries for file timestamps and UserDefaults, and the active app manifest includes the file as a resource. That verifies packaging intent at the source level, not the contents of a built archive or the correctness of every declaration. Inspect dependency manifests and the distribution artifact during real release validation. Apple can update required categories and accepted reasons, so use current official documentation for the exact policy at submission time.

Threat modeling is useful only if it changes delivery. Convert top risks into acceptance criteria and assign an owner for residual risk. Prefer a small verified control over a sweeping claim of “secure.” Record why a protection class, logging schema, or link restriction was selected and what would trigger reconsideration.

For staff practice, make the review reusable: a data-flow inventory, synthetic telemetry capture checklist, or Keychain failure taxonomy can help multiple teams. The artifact should make ordinary safe behavior easier while keeping decisions visible.

quiz.question: Does storing a token as a Keychain generic-password item make it a Secure Enclave key?
options: No; item storage and supported Secure Enclave key operations are different facilities
Yes, every String is converted to an enclave key
Only if the account attribute is localized
quiz.explanation: Keychain protects several item types. Secure Enclave use has specific supported key and access-control semantics; a generic-password secret is not automatically transformed into such a key.

quiz.question: What is the important consequence of WhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly for a foreground secret?
options: It makes the item readable before first unlock after every reboot
It restricts access to an unlocked device and does not migrate the item to another device
It guarantees automatic server-side revocation on uninstall
quiz.explanation: The availability policy restricts device-state access, and ThisDeviceOnly affects restoration/migration. It does not establish a service revocation or uninstall cleanup protocol.

quiz.question: A privacy manifest is present in source control. What can you conclude?
options: Every SDK is compliant and all logs are redacted
Every permission prompt will appear automatically
There is a declaration to inspect; packaging and actual data behavior still require verification
quiz.explanation: Declarations, packaging, runtime permissions, and observed collection are separate concerns. Review the archive, dependency declarations, and real data flows before making stronger claims.

exercise.brief: Review a made-up reminder that opens from a link, reads a session secret, displays cached details, and exports diagnostics. Write five specific risks and the checks for their proposed controls.
steps: Name the assets and mark the external-link, service, storage, and diagnostic-export boundaries.
At each boundary, state what an attacker can do and one concrete failure that could follow.
Choose a Keychain access policy. Explain access while locked, foreground/background needs, and migration to another device.
Define permitted diagnostic fields and what account change clears before another account sees the screen.
Read the query attributes and privacy-resource packaging. Record unanswered questions with evidence instead of asserting an unverified vulnerability.
acceptance: Every risk has a concrete mitigation, owner, and verification
The client is not treated as the service's authorization authority
Token, appointment details, and arbitrary response bodies are excluded from proposed telemetry

RiskAccountable owner (proposed role)Mitigation and evidence
Crafted link selects an unauthorized reminderRoute feature lead with service authorization leadParse bounded route; service checks ownership; test foreign synthetic ID

The worked secret policy allows access while unlocked on this device only, if credentials are needed only in the foreground. That choice accepts reauthentication after migration to another device. A later background requirement would need a new access-policy decision. Check the available classes and the feature's exposure needs before weakening a shared wrapper. The table above assigns a proposed owner and concrete evidence to each risk.

The event schema includes a bounded route category, outcome code, build, and duration bucket. It excludes the raw link, token, reminder text, and patient identity. Any needed correlation ID has a separate retention and access decision. Cleanup clears the visible model and account-scoped cache, performs narrowly scoped credential deletion when appropriate, and coordinates service revocation independently.

The repo review notes that Query.Attribute lacks an explicit accessibility case, while Apple's documented default is when-unlocked. It asks which consumers need background access rather than declaring a defect. The privacy file is referenced by the active Tuist manifest, but the final archive and dependency coverage remain unverified in this lab. This is a completed worked risk-register example, not an audit certification for the real application.

These are proposed accountable roles, not confirmed company maintainers or approvals. The route lead collects rejected-link fixtures and the service lead owns authorization evidence; telemetry owns exported captures; credential platform owns the status/accessibility matrix; account/session owns invalidation through the final commit; release owns archive contents. Each owner records an evidence location, review date, residual risk, and stop/recovery condition. A missing owner blocks acceptance of that row. Specialist review participates in the decision without leaving accountability as “the team.”

The note reaching the front desk does not give it authority. The desk checks who owns that locker. It also keeps key codes in a restricted drawer and records only whether a request succeeded, not the codes themselves. Locking the drawer helps, but it would not help if staff copied its contents onto the public noticeboard. Each step needs its own access and disclosure rule.

lessons.title: Release an app: follow the build, signing, and recovery steps
lessons.summary: Follow a commit to the exact distributed app. Keep signing inputs, resources, tests, and symbols linked, and describe what each recovery action can really change.
objectives: Explain the certificate/private-key pair, App ID, profile, and signed capabilities.
Tell apart source manifests, generated projects, and the test and archive paths still in use.
Link the commit, archive, symbols, build identity, and rollout evidence.
Tell apart pausing rollout, disabling a compatible feature, restoring a service, and shipping a corrective app version.

sections.title: Follow the app from source to installation
sections.html:
An artifact is a produced file or bundle, such as a build or archive. Follow the source and pinned dependencies through configuration, compilation, signing, export, upload, review, and availability. Android APK and app-bundle experience gives a starting map, but iOS steps and identity rules differ. A simulator run checks only part of this path. It does not show that the device archive contains the right resources, has the right capabilities, or is ready for someone to install from the distribution service.

A scheme selects targets and actions; a configuration selects settings such as Debug or Release. An archive is not simply a renamed simulator build. Device architecture, optimization, resources, entitlements, signing, and export configuration affect the final product. Extensions and App Clips also have identities and capabilities that must align with their containing app.

An artifact ledger is a record linking the commit, dependency lockfiles, toolchain, scheme/configuration, bundle ID, marketing version, build string, archive path, symbol UUIDs, test results, and distribution state. Keep these facts together so a crash can be traced to the exact binary. Passing unit tests does not establish which resources or environment were packaged in a different archive. Retain evidence for that final product separately.

These are operational distinctions, not ceremonies to memorize. When an installation fails, identify which boundary failed before regenerating every certificate or clearing caches.

sections.title: Match the signing identity and permitted capabilities
sections.html:
A signing identity pairs a certificate with its private key. The certificate alone cannot sign the app. An App ID names the application and registered capabilities. A provisioning profile states an allowed combination of signing identity, app identity, capabilities, and distribution type. Development and ad hoc profiles also involve registered devices. Think of these as related inputs that must agree, rather than one interchangeable “signing file.” A missing key needs a different fix from a profile for the wrong bundle ID.

Entitlements are signed claims used for capabilities and access, such as app groups or Keychain access groups. A project's requested entitlements must agree with the profile and account configuration. A bundle-ID mismatch, expired profile, missing key, unavailable capability, and missing device registration are different failures. Diagnose the actual message and relevant metadata rather than treating them all as “Xcode signing trouble.”

Automatic signing lets Xcode manage parts of provisioning; it does not remove the need for account access and valid capabilities. Distribution workflows can intentionally use explicit profiles and export settings. Keep private keys and account credentials in the approved secret store and bound their CI access. Rotating or revoking identities affects other consumers, so it is not a casual troubleshooting step.

The simulator also complicates simplistic advice. The checkout's Tuist CI comments explicitly preserve ad hoc signing of test hosts because Keychain tests fail without the expected entitlement context. Do not add CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED=NO universally merely because a test uses the simulator.

sections.title: Change the manifest that generates the project
sections.html:
A manifest is an input file describing a project and dependencies. Tuist reads Swift manifests and generates Xcode projects and workspaces from them. That purpose resembles Gradle, but Tuist's ProjectDescription API belongs to its tooling environment. Project.swift is not ordinary app code to compile with plain swiftc. Edit the source inputs that will survive regeneration. Also follow the actual workflow: a generated test workspace and a submission archive can still come from different paths during migration.

In this checkout, active feature and infrastructure manifests coexist with Package.swift files during migration. The app manifest is named Zocdoc-Tuist, and comments explain test-plan target identity dependencies. Read actual workflows before assuming all delivery has moved: tuist_build.yml generates and tests the Tuist graph, while the inspected submission workflow still archives Zocdoc.xcworkspace. Documentation can state an intended end state while current automation remains transitional.

Edit manifests and committed dependency inputs rather than generated project files. Resolve changed dependencies with the repository's pinned tools, then regenerate. The swift-tools-version header in a package manifest controls manifest/tool compatibility; it is not the same as every target's Swift language mode or minimum iOS deployment version. Those settings can vary across the graph.

Checkout facts verified on 2026-10-26: the inspected app target has an iOS 17.0 deployment minimum, CI selects Xcode 26.5 and simulator 26.5, and mise pins Tuist 4.203.4. These are repository settings, not claims about the latest Apple tools, every target's language mode, or the course snippets' minimum API versions. Re-read the linked pins when working on another revision.

Cache correctness is part of build correctness. The CI hashes dependency manifests, resolution pins, and tool configuration. Its Tuist scratch-cache restore intentionally uses exact matching to avoid stale dependency state. A cache hit accelerates delivery only if its inputs describe the artifact accurately.

sections.title: Keep CI results and the files behind them
sections.html:
Continuous integration, or CI, runs repeatable build and test work. Its evidence includes the exact toolchain, resolved pins, generated workspace, destination, products, and results. The checkout's Tuist workflow builds for testing, then tests those same products without rebuilding. An .xcresult is the result bundle that preserves details useful for investigation. A green icon says a job passed; the retained files and selected graph show which product and checks actually passed.

Release CI must retain the archive and matching dSYMs. The inspected submission workflow saves its archive, exports it, and uploads symbols to Sentry. Inspect retention and upload results during real operations; the existence of those steps alone does not prove that a particular run preserved its artifacts.

struct SyntheticReleaseIdentity: Equatable {
    let bundleID: String
    let marketingVersion: String
    let build: String
    let commit: String
}

let candidate = SyntheticReleaseIdentity(
    bundleID: "example.course.synthetic",
    marketingVersion: "1.2.1",
    build: "410",
    commit: "synthetic-commit"
)

This is standalone Swift metadata, not a signing tool. Swift synthesizes equality because all stored fields are equatable. The initializer's argument labels force each identity field to be explicit. Equality here means these strings match; it does not prove binary equivalence, signature validity, or API compatibility. Add binary UUIDs to the actual artifact ledger rather than using the marketing version as a symbol lookup key.

sections.title: Separate beta access from store release
sections.html:
TestFlight is Apple's beta distribution path through App Store Connect. Uploading a build, finishing processing, making it available to testers, completing any required beta review, passing App Review, and making it available in production are different states. Internal and external testers have different access and review paths. Apple's references checked on 2026-10-26 describe a 90-day test period for a build. Recheck current rules before real delivery. Upload success does not imply that anyone can install the build immediately.

Use beta validation for installation, upgrade from an older build, permissions, account transitions, crash reporting, and the actual production-like configuration. Simulator fixtures are valuable but cannot replace device installation and distribution-path checks. When testing environment-dependent behavior, record the exact build and configuration rather than assuming every TestFlight build targets production services.

Apple's phased release offers an update gradually over seven days to eligible users with automatic updates. Anyone can still manually download the available update. The phased percentage therefore does not bound the total number of installed clients or define your feature-flag cohort. A server-side experiment and a store rollout are separate control planes.

The local release guide describes release candidates, QA, manual release, and phased availability. Read it as the checkout's documented workflow, then verify current ownership and status during real delivery. No learning exercise authorizes uploading a build, changing store state, or sending release announcements.

sections.title: Say exactly which recovery action you mean
sections.html:
Recovery can mean stopping more rollout, disabling a compatible feature, restoring a service contract, or shipping a corrective version. These actions affect different clients. Apple's documentation checked on 2026-10-26 says a released App Store version cannot be reverted to an earlier version; you must submit a new version. Pausing phased release stops its further automatic progression, not installed copies. The same checked documentation permits pauses totaling 30 days. Recheck current limits before operations, and account for users who can still download manually.

A remote flag can disable a compatible feature on clients that read and honor it. It cannot rewrite bundled code, recover a failure before configuration loads, or guarantee immediate effect for an offline client using cached configuration. A backend rollback can restore service behavior only while its contract remains compatible with all installed clients. A destructive database migration may require repair or a forward migration rather than a literal rollback.

A corrective app release can reuse known-good source behavior, but it is a newly built, versioned, signed, tested, and reviewed artifact. It carries new symbol identity and delivery delay. Removing an app from sale does not repair existing installations, and its effects on phased-release availability require separate consideration.

Make recovery promises specific: who pauses distribution, who controls flags, which clients are affected, what happens offline, which data formats remain readable, who creates the corrective binary, and what evidence allows resumption. This is the iOS counterpart to a serious release runbook, not a single “rollback” button.

The worked ledger links made-up version 1.2.1 build 410 to its bundle ID, commit, dependency pins, Xcode, scheme/configuration, archive, binary UUIDs, matching dSYMs, results, and QA notes. The source shows Tuist tests using their generated graph while submission archives Zocdoc.xcworkspace. Actual run links, archive contents, and device observations stay pending until collected. A ledger records those gaps rather than treating source configuration as an executed release.

Signing readiness checks the certificate/private-key pair, App ID, profile distribution type, bundle IDs for app and extensions, and requested entitlements. Archive validation checks the intended Info.plist, privacy resources, environment settings, and symbols. A clean install and an upgrade from an older compatible build are separate acceptance cases.

FailureRecovery plan
Launch trap before configurationPause phased progression; diagnose matching crash; build and submit corrective version; remote flag cannot protect pre-config launch

The release captain owns distribution state, the feature owner owns safe client containment, and the service owner owns backward-compatible responses. Resumption requires confirmed task outcomes and diagnostics for the affected cohort, not simply a green build. This tabletop runbook describes decisions; it does not claim build 410 exists, signing was validated, or any TestFlight or App Store action was executed.
