lessons.title: Migration lab: propose a small change and prove its behavior
lessons.summary: Write a proposal for one made-up slot-mapping change. Compare full results, plan measurements, and keep accessibility, privacy, build, and recovery promises visible.
objectives: Write an RFC that names a concrete problem and what callers must observe.
Use an adapter to preserve callers while comparing old and new implementations.
Carry accessibility, performance, reliability, privacy, and build rules through the change.
Label a worked proposal separately from an improvement you have run, measured, or released.

sections.title: Start the proposal with one costly behavior
sections.html:
An RFC is a request for comments: a proposal that asks others to review a decision. Start with a concrete problem. Here a made-up mapper removes duplicate slot IDs while keeping each first slot. It repeatedly scans an array, which can cost more as the input grows. The proposed alternative uses a set for membership behind a clear contract. This is a synthetic problem for practice. It is not a claim that this particular defect or mapper exists in the checkout.

Write the problem as an observable statement: large result fixtures can incur expensive membership scans; ordering must remain stable; consumers need a seam for equivalence testing. Identify the scope and non-goals, including no persistence change, no booking side effects, and no UI framework migration. These boundaries prevent a small performance hypothesis from expanding into unrelated platform work.

An RFC is a decision artifact. Its reader needs the trigger, constraints, alternatives, recommended option, evidence, rollout, and unresolved questions. Name the owners and affected consumers. Do not demand consensus on every implementation detail, but obtain review from the people accountable for contracts that change. A concise decision log is more useful than an enormous document without a conclusion.

sections.title: Write the exact input and output rule
sections.html:
A pure operation depends only on its input and has no external side effects. This mapper reads an array and returns complete first-occurrence slots in input order. It neither waits nor touches storage or a server. If two slots share an ID but have different titles, keep the first title as well as the first ID. An ID is not an array index. State these rules before comparing performance so a faster candidate cannot silently change what the caller receives.

struct SyntheticSlot: Equatable, Sendable {
    let id: String
    let title: String
}

protocol SlotMapping {
    func map(_ slots: [SyntheticSlot]) -> [SyntheticSlot]
}

struct FirstOccurrenceMapper: SlotMapping {
    func map(_ slots: [SyntheticSlot]) -> [SyntheticSlot] {
        var seen = Set<String>()
        return slots.filter { seen.insert($0.id).inserted }
    }
}

This is standalone Swift using value types. Equatable permits complete-value comparisons; synthesized equality compares both fields. Sendable describes values whose stored fields support safe transfer under Swift concurrency checking; it does not run mapping on another actor. The protocol has no AnyObject constraint, so structs can conform. The underscore removes the external label from map.

No async appears because the operation does not suspend. If measurements later justify moving CPU work across isolation boundaries, that is a separate execution-policy decision. A thread-safe value model does not establish a scheduling policy or cancellation contract by itself.

sections.title: Put the old behavior behind a small adapter
sections.html:
An adapter gives callers one agreed API while connecting it to an existing implementation. Here callers receive a SlotMapping dependency chosen at construction. A scratch adapter can store a closure ([SyntheticSlot]) -> [SyntheticSlot]: it takes an array and returns an array. That closure may capture state, so review it before crossing actors. The synchronous protocol does not promise that every conforming implementation is Sendable. The adapter's job is compatibility, not an unstated concurrency guarantee.

Keep both implementations available until consumers and tests establish equivalence. This is the conceptual role of an Android interface adapter, not a claim that iOS requires a particular DI framework. The checkout's PrivacyChoicesModule illustrates a real module contract with @MainActor and coordinator factories. It is an example of an intentional UI boundary; do not attach UI isolation to a pure mapper merely because another protocol has it.

Shadow comparison is safe here only because the operation is pure. Run old and new mapping on the same synthetic input and compare results without exporting input content. Never duplicate a booking submission, account deletion, or other side-effecting operation in order to compare implementations. For those workflows, equivalence needs a different plan.

Choose how implementation selection occurs: local test injection first, then an appropriate production composition change if approved. A remote flag is optional and adds complexity. State when the old adapter will be removed; an indefinitely maintained duplicate path is a migration cost, not free insurance.

Here is the missing concrete old-path adapter and an executable characterization function. Add it after the declarations in the contract section in a standalone scratch Swift file; explicitly call verifySlotPrototype() under ordinary assertions. The old behavior is a synthetic scan, not copied client code:

struct ExistingSlotAdapter: SlotMapping {
    let legacy: ([SyntheticSlot]) -> [SyntheticSlot]
    func map(_ slots: [SyntheticSlot]) -> [SyntheticSlot] {
        legacy(slots)
    }
}

func scanningSlots(_ slots: [SyntheticSlot]) -> [SyntheticSlot] {
    var output: [SyntheticSlot] = []
    for slot in slots where !output.contains(where: { $0.id == slot.id }) {
        output.append(slot)
    }
    return output
}

func verifySlotPrototype() {
    let old: any SlotMapping = ExistingSlotAdapter(legacy: scanningSlots)
    let candidate: any SlotMapping = FirstOccurrenceMapper()
    let a = SyntheticSlot(id: "a", title: "First")
    let b = SyntheticSlot(id: "b", title: "Second")
    let changedA = SyntheticSlot(id: "a", title: "Replacement")
    let upperA = SyntheticSlot(id: "A", title: "Uppercase")
    let fixtures: [([SyntheticSlot], [SyntheticSlot])] = [
        ([], []), ([a, changedA], [a]), ([a, b], [a, b]),
        ([a, b, changedA], [a, b]), ([upperA, a], [upperA, a])
    ]
    for (input, expected) in fixtures {
        precondition(old.map(input) == expected)
        precondition(candidate.map(input) == expected)
        precondition(old.map(input) == candidate.map(input))
    }
    let selectedID = "a"
    let reordered = candidate.map([b, a, changedA])
    precondition(reordered.first { $0.id == selectedID } == a)
}

The adapter's stored closure provides the old scan through the same synchronous protocol. Each fixture has expected complete values written independently, so two wrong implementations cannot pass merely by agreeing. Conflicting titles detect a last-title mistake. Uppercase IDs detect unwanted normalization. Selection after reorder checks identity rather than index. Successful assertion execution establishes those fixture behaviors. It does not measure memory, accessibility, screen delay, or the final build graph.

sections.title: Preserve the promises around the mapper
sections.html:
Functional equivalence means preserving what callers and people can observe. A stable order helps keep focus and selection predictable. An ID names the slot; the localized title presents it. If selection stores an array index, changing the array can point it at a different slot. Check the selected ID after a reorder or replacement instead. That is a consumer contract question for the prototype, not evidence of an existing checkout bug. The mapper must fit the surrounding accessibility and data rules too.

Accessibility acceptance covers focus after results update, selected-state announcements, and the largest supported text size. Localization ownership stays with the presenting target; this mapper should not manufacture English sentences or change date-zone policy. Performance acceptance covers equivalent fixtures, release configuration, interval boundaries, and memory overhead from membership storage.

Reliability acceptance includes empty input, all duplicates, conflicting duplicate titles, and no-response states at the surrounding data boundary. The pure mapper itself cannot resolve a timed-out submission. Observability may record a bounded mapping version and duration bucket; it should not export slot titles or patient context.

Build integration must include the source and tests in the active manifest graph. The booking and module manifests in this checkout define sources, dependencies, and test targets. During coexistence, prove that the relevant test graph and archive graph both include the intended implementation. One graph's green status is not a universal compatibility certificate.

sections.title: Compare three options and a reason to change your mind
sections.html:
An alternative is another way to address the same problem. Option A keeps the scan and adds tests. It may be enough for small inputs. Option B uses a membership set while preserving the old output, trading extra storage for less expected search work. Option C moves mapping across an async boundary, adding lifetime and cancellation decisions. Compare all three against representative inputs and the user-visible interval. A preferred option should still have a stated result that would make you reject it.

Recommend B provisionally only after representative measurements and full-value equivalence checks support it. Do not treat asymptotic analysis as a measured user benefit. Say what would change the decision: negligible screen-level benefit, problematic memory growth, differing duplicate semantics, or lack of a clean consumer seam.

List risks with mitigations and residual limits. A fixture missing conflicting duplicates can let a semantic regression pass; add that fixture. A CI microbenchmark can be noisy; preserve raw samples and validate on a device. A production telemetry field can leak content; allowlist bounded fields and review captures. An older app may continue using the old mapper after rollout, so service contracts must tolerate both.

The decision record should distinguish rejected alternatives from unresolved ones. You can defer async execution intentionally without asserting that it is wrong for every feature.

sections.title: Use evidence gates and an end date
sections.html:
A milestone is a step with a result you can inspect. First record the old behavior with fixtures whose expected values are known. Add the contract and adapter, then the candidate. Compare full values before measuring. Check both isolated mapping and the person's delay. Integrate through construction and the relevant build graphs. Plan observation and removal of the redundant path. Give each milestone an evidence gate, an owner, and an exit condition so temporary migration code does not become permanent by accident.

Each milestone should state its go/no-go criterion and artifact: equivalence test results, trace, source-graph review, resource/build validation, or rollout dashboard. A checkbox without an attached observation remains a plan. Define a migration budget so temporary abstractions and duplicate tests do not persist indefinitely.

Containment selects the old pure implementation only on clients that contain and honor that selection mechanism. It does not downgrade an installed app, undo a persisted format, or repair earlier side effects. This lab deliberately avoids changing persistence so that its recovery story remains small. If the real proposal requires a schema change, add backward-read/write compatibility and data-repair reasoning explicitly.

End the RFC with a decision request: approve the behavior contract and experimental rollout under the stated evidence gates. Do not ask reviewers to approve an unbounded migration. A staff-quality proposal makes both the expected benefit and the cost of being wrong understandable.

options: The value's stored fields support safe transfer under concurrency checking

quiz.explanation: Sendable concerns transfer and shared-state safety. It neither selects an executor nor makes all implementations of an unrelated protocol sendable.

options: Claim the entire screen is faster anyway
Remove all measurements
Reassess the user benefit and inspect the remaining end-to-end costs
quiz.explanation: The hypothesis may be true locally while irrelevant to the user delay. Revisit the recommendation and remaining costs rather than promoting a narrow benchmark into a broader claim.

exercise.brief: Write an RFC and scratch prototype for first-occurrence slot mapping. Deliver the decision, exact expected fixtures, evidence plan, and recovery limits. Leave client sources untouched.
steps: State the problem, affected callers, scope exclusions, and exact first-value and ordering rules.
Describe the old adapter and candidate behind SlotMapping.

exercise.solution:
The worked RFC is titled “Keep first-occurrence slot mapping behind a tested value contract.” It asks about a synthetic large-list membership cost. The scope excludes UI replacement, storage-format changes, and network submissions. Its contract preserves input order, case-sensitive IDs, and each first complete slot without mutating the input. These exact promises make the proposal reviewable before any timing or rollout claim.

The equivalence fixture contains a/First, b/Second, and a/Replacement; expected output is the first two complete values. Comparing IDs alone would miss an accidental last-title policy. Empty, all-duplicate, and all-distinct inputs complete the minimal matrix. A separate consumer test changes the array order while preserving a selected ID, then verifies the selection still points to that ID.

Option B is provisionally selected over unchanged scans and new async scheduling. The measurement plan compares several input sizes, records release/device conditions and memory cost, and then measures action-to-usable-results. Until those observations exist, the benefit is a hypothesis. The proposed dependency seam follows the concept of the actual module protocol, while the pure mapper remains free of UI actor annotations.

Milestones are characterize, adapt, implement, compare, measure, integrate, observe, and remove. Characterization requires expected full-value results; integration requires source/test inclusion in both relevant graphs during coexistence. Rollout records mapping-version cohorts using approved bounded telemetry. Containment uses the old pure implementation only if the installed binary contains an honored selection path. Removal requires stable outcomes and owner agreement that the duplicate path is no longer needed.

The decision request is approval for this bounded experiment, not approval for a completed migration. The evidence ledger marks device accessibility, end-to-end timing, archive verification, and production impact as planned. A reviewable proposal with those limits is useful even before implementation; it must not be presented as observed team or customer impact.

Use ExistingSlotAdapter, scanningSlots, and verifySlotPrototype from the adapter section as the worked prototype, with the shared SyntheticSlot and FirstOccurrenceMapper declarations. Run the five expected-value fixtures before timing either implementation. Record the actual invocation and outcome; source text alone leaves equivalence execution pending. A successful migration retires the old scan and temporary adapter after adoption and recovery review. Rejecting the experiment retires the candidate instead. Name the mapper owner for that debt and keep only the selected permanent contract.

lessons.summary: Use course artifacts to show what you can explain, reproduce, and own. Label gaps and planned work honestly, then choose the next task that supplies missing evidence.
objectives: Explain an unfamiliar iOS path using types, state ownership, isolation, and build evidence.
Tell apart a plan, a reproduced behavior, a production result, and an observed team benefit.
Review a portfolio with concrete questions and explicit evidence limits.
Build a development plan around demonstrated gaps and needed responsibilities rather than a list of frameworks.

sections.title: Build evidence of judgment and impact
sections.html:
Judgment is choosing a useful action and explaining its reasons and limits. Your Android experience already brings debugging, product, and collaboration habits. Now make those habits reliable in iOS situations: value and reference lifetimes, actor access, UI behavior, diagnostics, and distribution. A portfolio is a small set of artifacts that shows those decisions and their evidence. Knowing API names helps, but the goal is to handle the whole bounded task and its failure cases with accountable choices.

Completing this course does not guarantee a staff title, promotion, or exhaustive platform expertise. Organizations evaluate scope, consistency, influence, and results within their own expectations. Use the course as a way to acquire and demonstrate technical competence, then build actual evidence of sustained team and customer impact.

A valuable portfolio connects a problem, decision, implementation, verification, outcome, and wider effect. A tutorial exercise supports learning; a reproduced defect supports diagnosis; a deployed improvement supports an operational outcome; a reusable practice adopted by another team supports influence. These are related but different claims.

Choose a bounded next responsibility, such as independently delivering a feature across the iOS lifecycle with a reliable review and release path. Then expand scope through measured improvements, mentoring, and cross-team contracts. Do not replace an honest learning gap with a stronger title in the artifact's description.

sections.title: Explain the small distinctions that change behavior
sections.html:
Ownership answers who keeps state or work alive and who ends its lifetime. A reviewer can ask why a model is a struct or class, which references retain a controller, and whether a closure outlives its caller. Explain actor isolation as an access rule, a Task as work that can pause, await as a possible wait, and Sendable as a transfer-safety promise. These distinctions affect correctness. None of these words alone means that code runs on a background thread.

For UI work, trace state ownership, presentation lifetime, dismissal, navigation, and error rendering. A SwiftUI body describes a view value; it is not an Android activity callback. UIKit lifecycle behavior needs its own reasoning, particularly when embedded into or hosting SwiftUI. Ask how a screen behaves after data changes while visible, not just at initial construction.

For data work, distinguish absent optional data from invalid data, a thrown error from a fatal trap, cancellation from a failed server operation, and transport success from product success. For resources, distinguish a package's bundle from the main bundle, locale from time zone, and scalable font size from paragraph geometry.

These questions expose competence better than a framework inventory. Use local code to support an answer: the booking-title helper demonstrates paragraph behavior, the module protocol demonstrates UI isolation, and the workflows demonstrate transitional build graphs. State where the evidence stops instead of extrapolating to the whole app.

sections.title: Mark what you planned and what you actually checked
sections.html:
A claim is a statement your evidence must support. “I wrote a measurement plan” and “I measured this screen” are different claims. Label entries as planned, observed, or reproduced so a reader cannot accidentally treat a design as a result. The small standalone Swift model below records that distinction with a fixed enum and a text claim. It is a bookkeeping aid for a portfolio, not a scoring algorithm for a job title or proof of independent delivery.

enum EvidenceState: String {
    case planned, observed, reproduced
}

struct PortfolioEntry {
    let claim: String
    let state: EvidenceState
    let artifact: String
    let limitation: String
}

let entry = PortfolioEntry(
    claim: "Stable order preserved in synthetic mapping fixture",
    state: .planned,
    artifact: "mapping-equivalence-test",
    limitation: "Execution result and device impact not yet attached"
)

The enum restricts the vocabulary. A String raw value provides a readable label if needed. Stored let fields make each entry immutable after construction; revising a claim creates a new value or updates it through a deliberately mutable owner. The inferred .planned case is known from the initializer parameter type.

An observed result records what happened under specified conditions. A reproduced result has enough setup and repetition to support another engineer's investigation, but still may not establish production causality. Neither status alone proves broad impact. Add the method, fixture, environment, result artifact, and residual uncertainty.

Keep separate entries when the scopes differ: “isolated mapper is faster on a device” and “users reach results sooner” require different measurements. Likewise, “a checklist exists” and “another team adopted it and avoided a recurring failure” are different influence claims.

sections.title: Connect a small set of useful artifacts
sections.html:
An artifact is something another person can inspect, such as a trace, test result, or review note. Choose a connected set. Begin with a feature trace from entry point through state, service, UI, and tests. Add data contract tests, accessibility and language checks, a performance report, incident note, threat model, release runbook, and RFC. Make shared assumptions explicit so the pieces agree. A performance claim and release plan should refer to the same relevant build and behavior rather than tell unrelated stories.

For each artifact, name your contribution and collaborators. If a teammate diagnosed the issue or owns the build system, say so. A credible portfolio explains what you decided, what evidence you collected, and how the team used the result. Private company code or customer data must stay within its authorized context; use synthetic excerpts and permitted links for any wider sharing.

Outcome descriptions need denominators and time windows. “Reduced crashes” is incomplete without build/cohort, reporting coverage, and incidence. “Improved launch” needs a launch definition, device/configuration, sample count, and distribution. “Improved team delivery” needs an observable adoption or reduced-cost signal, not just a polished document.

You can include unfinished learning work if it is clearly labeled. A thoughtful unresolved question and a concrete experiment can demonstrate judgment. Do not fill the portfolio with invented production metrics to make every artifact look finished.

sections.title: Use a review to find what you can own next
sections.html:
A review conversation tests reasoning under changing conditions. Use three tasks: explain an unfamiliar local path and its failures; defend an RFC choice and a condition that would reverse it; and walk through an imagined incident from evidence to containment and recovery. A tabletop incident is a discussion, not an executed production response. Let the reviewer change one assumption, such as offline flags, longer text, or a different archive graph, and explain how your decisions change.

Calibrate readiness by observed independence and scope. Can you execute the bounded work with normal code review? Can you diagnose failures outside the happy path? Can you identify when an infrastructure or privacy owner must participate? Can another engineer reproduce the artifact without the original conversation? These questions assess responsibility; they do not automatically map to a company rank.

Record gaps concretely. “Needs more iOS experience” is too vague. “Can explain the manifest but has not validated a device archive or upgrade path” leads to a useful next exercise. “Knows cancellation syntax but suppresses timeout ambiguity” identifies a design gap. Agree on a representative next task and the evidence that would demonstrate improvement.

Mentoring matters because it exposes hidden assumptions. Have a teammate reproduce your benchmark or trace a resource lookup using your notes. If they need undocumented setup, improve the artifact before claiming it scales across the team.

The review can conclude “pending.” In the supplied portfolio, device accessibility, full-screen timing, archive checks, and team adoption are still planned. A reviewer can choose a supervised scratch investigation next, then reconsider a bounded delivery task when its evidence exists. Record the proposed scope, missing checks, accountable reviewer, and next review date. A thoughtful design does not, by itself, establish independent execution or readiness for release decisions.

sections.title: Choose two concrete gaps and how to close them
sections.html:
A development gap is missing evidence or skill for the responsibility you want to take. Choose two gaps with a high cost in your likely work. For a first iOS feature, device debugging and archive validation may matter more than learning a specialist framework. For a platform role, module boundaries and migration measurement may be more useful. Name the missing observation, the next task, the reviewer, and what result would close the gap. Revisit the plan after that evidence exists.

Write a plan with an artifact, reviewer, completion evidence, and time to revisit it. For example: reproduce a lifecycle cancellation case in an isolated target, collect a matching diagnostic, and explain its state transition to a teammate. Then independently own a bounded feature with accessibility acceptance and a reviewed release path. Later assess whether a shared guideline has reduced repeated review findings.

Keep evidence current. Repository anchors are verified for this checkout, but line numbers and build workflows evolve. Before real implementation, re-read the manifest and active workflow rather than relying on a course screenshot. API availability, toolchain pins, privacy requirements, and store processes likewise need current sources when the decision is made.

Finish with a clear handoff: what you can own now, where you need review, what remains unverified, and which next task closes the gap. That is useful to a manager, mentor, and teammate. It makes progress visible without pretending that a seven-session production unit is a substitute for sustained platform practice.

quiz.question: Which statement is a defensible claim after finishing the synthetic performance lab?
options: The production app is definitely faster for all users
A benchmark design and behavior contract exist; measured outcomes require executed evidence
A staff promotion is guaranteed
quiz.explanation: The artifact supports learning and planned verification. Production benefit and organizational level require different evidence; neither follows from completing an exercise.

quiz.question: A reviewer asks whether the isolated mapping result proves faster first usable results. What should the portfolio show?
options: Separate entries and measurements for the isolated and end-to-end boundaries
One merged metric with no fixture details
Only the most favorable run
quiz.explanation: A narrow benchmark and a user-visible outcome have different boundaries and causes. Connecting them requires an appropriate end-to-end experiment, not a stronger label.

quiz.question: Which development-plan item best addresses an actual gap?
options: Learn every Apple framework
Become staff by the end of the month
Validate an upgrade archive on a device with a reviewer and retain the artifact ledger
quiz.explanation: The device-archive task has a bounded responsibility, reviewer, and observable evidence. Framework inventories and rank promises do not identify a concrete competence gap.

exercise.brief: Review your course portfolio before handing off a bounded iOS responsibility. Make an evidence ledger, review script, and plan for two gaps. Mark missing observations explicitly.
steps: List the feature trace, tests, accessibility matrix, performance report, incident note, threat model, release ledger, and RFC.
Mark each claim planned, observed, or reproduced. Attach actual evidence when it exists.
Choose one local path and explain its ownership, isolation, failures, and build inclusion.
Discuss a faulty launch before remote configuration while older clients remain installed.
Choose two demonstrated gaps. Give each a next artifact, reviewer, and completion check.
Write what you can own now, where you need review, and what remains unverified.
acceptance: Learning artifacts are not presented as production or promotion outcomes
Every outcome claim has an evidence source and scope
The review addresses small syntax and platform distinctions as well as architecture
Recovery reasoning respects installed-client and App Store limits
The plan is bounded, reviewable, and connected to demonstrated gaps
exercise.solution:
The worked index lists eight artifacts: feature trace, contract tests, accessibility matrix, mapping measurement, incident note, threat model, release ledger, and RFC. Each entry names its claim, scope, evidence status, reviewer, and gap. Supplied designs do not prove production outcomes. Reasoning through synthetic fixtures is useful, but it does not create a customer metric or prove that a learner independently ran the practice.

ClaimEvidence requiredCurrent example status
Slot order is preservedExecuted full-value equivalence fixturesPlanned until results attached
UI remains usable with large textDevice task audit plus visual and trait-update checksPlanned
Mapper reduces user delayIsolated distribution and end-to-end device measurementPlanned; no production benefit claimed
Release is recoverableArtifact ledger and tested containment boundariesTabletop design only
Practice improves team deliveryAdoption and an observed cost or failure reductionNo team-impact claim yet

The mentor script asks: explain why attributed text can clip after font scaling; show where the active helper addresses it; explain why a DEBUG event callback is not a production redaction policy; distinguish the Tuist test graph from submission archive; and handle a launch trap before flags load. The answer pauses further phased progression, retains and matches symbols, diagnoses the trap, and plans a corrective release while maintaining compatible services for installed clients. It promises no downgrade.

Gap one is device artifact validation: produce a reviewed install/upgrade ledger for an authorized synthetic target and retain symbols and results. Gap two is cross-actor lifecycle reasoning: reproduce cancellation during a state transition and explain ownership and reconciliation. Completion means another engineer can follow the setup and assess the result. The handoff is conditional: “After the feature contract tests, representative interaction evidence, and peer reproduction are attached and accepted, the reviewer may recommend a bounded feature with ordinary review. Until then, independent delivery readiness remains unverified; release and privacy choices involve the established owners.” A later portfolio may add sustained delivery and team adoption evidence, but no title is inferred from this review.

simple.story: A bicycle mechanic keeps a notebook. One page sketches how to repair a brake. Another records a brake she repaired on a practice bicycle and the checks she ran. A third says a colleague followed her notes and repaired another bicycle without extra help. These pages show different things: a plan, an executed check, and useful transfer to someone else. The mechanic labels each page and keeps the parts and conditions clear. A neat sketch is valuable, but it does not become a road-tested repair merely by being placed in the notebook.
simple.meaning: A portfolio separates plans, observations, reproducible checks, production outcomes, and team adoption. Each claim needs evidence at the same scope, rather than a stronger label or invented metric.

example.before: The portfolio says “slot order is preserved,” marked planned. It contains source fixtures but no executed results.
example.change: Run the five expected-value fixtures in the scratch prototype and attach the command, environment, and passing output.
example.after: The entry now supports observed fixture behavior. It still does not establish production speed, device accessibility, or independent reproduction by another engineer.

simple.remember: Make the claim no larger than the evidence behind it.
simple.boundary: Repair notebooks explain evidence levels, not company promotion criteria. Passing scratch fixtures is learning evidence; staff responsibility also needs sustained delivery, collaboration, and observed impact.
